analysis.one_liner: Required clear cell phone contracts and bills and cut early termination fees.
analysis.headline: The cell phone consumer bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee after one hearing and never got a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced wireless carriers to disclose contract terms, fees, and taxes clearly before customers sign, publish county-level coverage maps, report dropped calls and dead zones to the FCC, prorate early termination fees so they shrink over the life of a two-year contract, limit how small changes can secretly extend a contract, and let troops deployed overseas cancel service without penalty. It died in the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Cell phone customers: the bill would have required plain-language contracts and bills with taxes and fees itemized separately, so people could compare plans and see which charges the carrier added on its own [S2][S3]. It would have prorated early termination fees — the record notes carriers charged $175 or more no matter whether a customer quit after a day or a year — given a 30-day right to cancel any new contract without penalty, and let subscribers leave without penalty when the carrier raised rates or worsened terms [S2][S3]. Rural customers would have gotten county-level coverage maps before signing, and deployed servicemembers could cancel contracts without penalty [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone customers, especially rural ones

how_it_helps.text: Early termination fees of $175 or more would have been prorated, dropping to at most half by the midpoint of a two-year contract, instead of staying the same whether a customer quit after a day or a year.

Contracts and ads would have had to disclose contract length, termination fees, per-minute charges, and taxes and surcharges in plain, tabular form before a customer signed, and carriers could not list discretionary fees in the tax-and-fee section of a bill.

Subscribers would have gotten a 30-day right to cancel any new contract without penalty, notice and a 30-day opt-out when a change extended their contract, and the right to leave without penalty if the carrier raised rates or cut service quality.

Carriers would have had to publish county-level service maps updated quarterly, and the FCC would have collected and published semiannual data on dropped calls and coverage dead zones, with a public complaint website.

Servicemembers ordered to deployments of 90 days or more could terminate a cell phone contract without penalty, with criminal penalties for carriers who tried to seize deposits to collect payments after termination.

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers — companies like the major national wireless providers — would bear the cost: prorated termination fees would shrink a fee that the bill's own findings describe as often disconnected from the actual cost of a phone, and disclosure rules would end the practice of burying discretionary surcharges in bills where customers cannot tell them from government taxes [S3]. Some carriers pass compliance costs to customers, though the disclosure rules are aimed at making those charges visible rather than banning them.

drawbacks.text: Carriers argued early termination fees subsidize handset costs — letting customers buy phones at a deep discount upfront in exchange for a two-year commitment — so prorating the fees could push more of the phone's true price to the point of sale. The bill acknowledged this by requiring the FCC to weigh the legitimate business reasons for the fees and the effect on competition when writing the rule.

The bill relies heavily on FCC rulemaking, with the agency writing the detailed formats, map standards, and fee-proration formula within 180 days, so the real-world protections would depend on how the FCC implemented them.
The bill preempts inconsistent state laws, though it exempts state laws that give customers more protection than the federal standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to customers are concrete and the costs to carriers are mostly transparency and foregone fee revenue, not higher prices by design: clearer bills and contracts, smaller termination fees, and an exit when terms worsen. The main legitimate tradeoff is that termination fees also financed subsidized phones, so prorating could shift some phone cost upfront. The bill is narrowly drawn and leaves carriers' core pricing freedom intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held one hearing on it, but the committee never approved it and the Senate never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the bill on September 7, 2007, with Sen. Rockefeller, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill.

The Commerce Committee held a hearing on October 17, 2007, with the hearing printed as S.Hrg. 110-1175, but the committee took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no Senate floor vote — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wireless carriers came out ahead: with no vote ever held, they kept flat early termination fees of $175 or more, contract extensions triggered by minor account changes, and the ability to list discretionary surcharges on bills without clear labeling, all of which the bill would have restricted.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require cell phone contract and bill disclosure, prorated early termination fees, coverage maps, and servicemember cancellation rights.

for.name: Sen. Jay Rockefeller
for.role: Senator from West Virginia; original co-introducer
for.what_they_did: Joined Klobuchar in introducing the bill in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill in October 2007 but never brought it to a markup or vote, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: CTIA - The Wireless Association
against.what_they_did: The wireless industry opposed federal restrictions on early termination fees and fought carrier regulation of this kind during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members stood; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled Commerce Committee heard but never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have prorated early termination fees of $175 or more, blocked contract extensions triggered by minor account changes, and forced disclosure of discretionary surcharges — cutting revenue streams built on customer lock-in and confusing bills. Carriers' financial interest ran against the customers the bill was protecting.

industries.industry: Handset makers and the subsidized-phone retail model
industries.note: Termination fees helped carriers subsidize handset prices, so prorating them could push more phone cost upfront, though the bill also directed the FCC to study handset locking, which limits consumers' ability to switch carriers with the phone they own.
